# Job Chapter 34 — The LOGOS Bible (Formal)
**Translator:** LOGOS | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 429r–429v

---

**1** Then Elihu answered and said: **2** "Hear my words, you wise men, and give ear to me, you who know. **3** For the ear tests words as the palate tastes food.

**4** Let us choose what is right; let us determine among ourselves what is good. **5** For Job has said, 'I am righteous, and God has taken away my right. **6** In spite of my right I am counted a liar; my wound is incurable, though I am without transgression.'

**7** What man is like Job, who drinks up scoffing like water, **8** who travels in company with evildoers and walks with wicked men? **9** For he has said, 'It profits a man nothing to take delight in God.'

**10** Therefore hear me, you men of understanding: far be it from God that he should do wickedness, and from the Almighty that he should do wrong. **11** For according to the work of a man he will repay him, and according to his ways he will make it befall him. **12** Of a truth, God will not do wickedly, and the Almighty will not pervert justice.

**13** Who gave him charge over the earth, and who laid on him the whole world? **14** If he should set his heart to it and gather to himself his spirit and his breath, **15** all flesh would perish together, and man would return to dust.

**16** If you have understanding, hear this; listen to what I say. **17** Shall one who hates justice govern? Will you condemn the Righteous Mighty One? **18** Who says to a king, 'Worthless one,' and to nobles, 'Wicked one'? **19** Who shows no partiality to princes, nor regards the rich more than the poor, for they are all the work of his hands?

**20** In a moment they die; at midnight the people are shaken and pass away, and the mighty are taken away by no human hand. **21** For his eyes are upon the ways of a man, and he sees all his steps. **22** There is no darkness or deep shadow where evildoers may hide themselves.

**23** For God has no need to consider a man further, that he should go before God in judgment. **24** He shatters the mighty without investigation and sets others in their place. **25** Thus, knowing their works, he overturns them in the night, and they are crushed. **26** He strikes them for their wickedness in a place where others see, **27** because they turned aside from following him and had no regard for any of his ways, **28** so that they caused the cry of the poor to come to him, and he heard the cry of the afflicted.

**29** When he is quiet, who can condemn? When he hides his face, who can behold him? He is over both nation and man alike, **30** so that a godless man should not reign, that there be no one to ensnare the people.

**31** For has anyone said to God, 'I have borne punishment; I will not offend anymore; **32** teach me what I do not see; if I have done iniquity, I will do it no more'?

**33** Should he then repay it according to your mind, because you reject his judgment? For you must choose, not I; so declare what you know.

**34** Men of understanding will say to me, and the wise man who hears me will say: **35** 'Job speaks without knowledge; his words are without insight.' **36** Would that Job were tested to the end, because of his answers in the manner of wicked men. **37** For he adds rebellion to his sin; he claps his hands among us and multiplies his words against God."

---
## LOGOS Translation Notes

**Verses 10-12 — The justice of God:** Elihu's central argument is stated plainly: God cannot do wickedness. This is not merely an assertion of divine goodness but a logical argument — the one who governs all creation cannot, by definition, pervert the justice he himself established.

**Verse 14-15 — God's sustaining breath:** If God withdrew his *ruach* (spirit/breath), all life would end instantly. This is not a threat but a reminder that existence itself is a continuous act of divine generosity. The argument is that the God who sustains every breath is not the tyrant Job imagines.

**Verse 29 — "When he is quiet, who can condemn?":** God's silence — which is precisely Job's complaint — is here reframed by Elihu as sovereign freedom. God is not obligated to answer. This is provocative theology that will be both confirmed and complicated when God finally does speak.

*— LOGOS*
